newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia says EU decision stimulus for reform.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia says EU decision stimulus for reform.

text.p: Slovenia said on Wednesday the European Commission's decision to invite it to start European Union entry talks next year would spur Ljubljana to continue on its reform path.

"This is a very positive move which acknowledges Slovenia's economic and political development and will be a stimulant to accelerate preparations for negotiations with the EU," said Marija Adanja, a senior official at the foreign ministry.
The Commission's opinion on Slovenia, published on Wednesday, would guide the former Yugoslav republic over the next months, she added.
"We will accelerate the harmonisation of our legislation with EU laws and speed up the reform of state administration."
Slovenia is one of five former communist states to receive invitations to enter negotiations with Brussels. It joins the Czech Republic, Poland, Hungary and Estonia as well as Cyprus.

Adanja said Slovenia hoped to become a full member of the EU by the year 2001 and forecast integration would boost the nation's economic development. Slovenia has already made huge strides towards Western European living standards.
"I expect a positive effect on the economy as a whole. It should promote investment," she said.
Trade with EU-member states, which already represents more than 65 percent of the country's total, was unlikely to increase significantly, however, accroding to Adanja.
Analysts were in broad agreement with the government's assessments of the benefit of closer EU ties.

"The commission's decision will force the government and the economy to speed up changes to bring the state administration and economy closer to European standards," said Peter Stanovnik, an economist at Ljubljana University.
He forecast the pace of privatisation would pick up, especially for banks and insurance companies.

"A lot of changes will be needed in the banking and insurance sectors which will have to adopt to tougher international competition. The price of financial services will have to fall significantly," he said.
Foreign investment would rise, stoked by the increased security EU membership would offer, he added.
"The economy needs foreign investment. It enhances know-how, management skills and international connections."
In 1996 direct foreign investments to Slovenia amounted to only $185.9 million or about one percent of GDP,
Share traders predicted the promise of eventual full EU membership would improve the stability and liquidity of Slovenian capital markets.
"The decision will improve stability, lure fresh foreign investors and push liquidity up," said Milos Pelcar, a trader at bank A banka.
